methodology: We implemented AC-AZT as a deterministic policy gateway and evaluated it on a controlled scenario-based benchmark containing 60 manually interpretable base actions and 240 total cases. The benchmark emphasizes cloud actions (30 bases) and includes 15 edge and 15 IoT transfer cases. Each action was evaluated under benign, instruction-injection, scope-escalation, and stale or unsafe-context conditions. An author-specified oracle, computed without calling any method, assigned PERMIT, APPROVAL_REQUIRED, or DENY from explicit security properties before the three mechanisms were run. Context records included identity, session, tool, evidence, rollback, delegation, approved scope, requested scope, post-condition state, and five normalized risk factors. We compared direct execution, a static role/action allowlist, and AC-AZT using unauthorized-action rate, legitimate-action success, attack success, escalation, false escalation, decision agreement, invariant violations, and local policy-engine timing. Six formal invariants tested authorization completeness, hard-rule dominance, capability confinement, freshness, delegation attenuation, and verified completion. Ablation removed one control at a time, whereas threshold and weight analyses examined policy calibration. The deterministic outcomes were analyzed descriptively as paired cases; case-level McNemar tests and Wilson intervals are exploratory only, repetitions were used only for timing, and all figures describe benchmark proportions rather than real-world incident frequencies.
results: Under the controlled cases, AC-AZT achieved a legitimate-action success rate of 93.9%, an unauthorized-action rate of 1.4%, and an adversarial attack-success rate of 0.0%. The corresponding unauthorized-action rates were 95.2% for direct execution and 67.1% for static authorization. AC-AZT's oracle decision agreement was 97.5%, compared with 17.9% and 40.0% for the baselines. Its false-escalation rate was 6.1%, showing the measured utility cost of the added control. AC-AZT recorded 0 violations across the six declared invariants, whereas direct execution and static authorization recorded 249 and 179, respectively. The adversarial result should not be read as a universal zero-attack claim: it reflects deterministic enforcement against the mutation classes represented here. The median local authorization time was 1.60 µs (95th percentile 1.80 µs); this value measures Python policy computation only and not end-to-end cloud, edge, or IoT response latency. These results support the hypothesis only within the defined scenario set: the gateway reduced unsafe execution while retaining most immediate actions that the oracle classified as safe. The remaining errors were boundary-case disagreements between the transparent risk threshold and the oracle, which exposes a calibration cost rather than hiding it.
ablation: Removing hard rules changed UAR from 1.4% to 42.0%, while removing contextual risk changed it to 3.9% and removing scope bounding changed it to 15.0%. Disabling verification changed the failed-effect commit rate from 0.0% to 30.0%. Removing the freshness check produced UAR 3.9%. Hard-rule removal had the largest safety effect because it disabled identity-, interface-, delegation-, rollback-, and protected-asset constraints simultaneously. Scope and freshness controls addressed narrower failure classes, whereas contextual risk primarily resolved boundary cases. Verification did not change pre-execution UAR, but it determined whether a failed effect was committed. The ablation therefore separates authorization from recovery rather than treating all controls as interchangeable.
sensitivity: Across permit thresholds 0.30–0.70, LASR ranged from 84.8% to 100.0%, while UAR ranged from 0.0% to 3.9%. The highest decision agreement in this controlled set occurred at threshold 0.35; this is a descriptive benchmark result, not a universal optimum. Across the six interpretable weight profiles, LASR ranged from 93.9% to 93.9%, and UAR ranged from 1.4% to 2.4%. The seeded Dirichlet analysis further shows how unconstrained organizational preferences can move decisions around the permit boundary. These findings support explicit policy calibration: a stricter threshold improves containment but can escalate safe actions, whereas a permissive threshold improves immediate utility at the cost of more oracle-non-permitted execution.
limitations: The benchmark is synthetic and controlled and does not estimate real incident frequencies. Agent reasoning and natural-language planning are outside scope, no production infrastructure is modified, and the risk factors and oracle judgments require external review and organizational calibration. Timing measures only local Python policy computation. The case author may introduce judgment bias, despite the oracle being implemented separately from the evaluated policy. The fixed action catalog cannot represent every chained, long-horizon, multi-agent, time-of-check/time-of-use, approval-quality, or cyberphysical failure. Human approval is modeled as a withheld token rather than a behavioral experiment. Consequently, the results demonstrate policy behavior under the evaluated conditions rather than universal safety, operational resilience, or deployment effectiveness.
abstract_update: We implement AC-AZT as a deterministic action-level authorization gateway and evaluate it on 240 controlled benign, adversarial, and failure cases across cloud, edge, and IoT settings. Compared with direct and static authorization, AC-AZT records 1.4% unauthorized-action rate while preserving 93.9% of oracle-permitted actions. Ablation and sensitivity analyses separate the contributions of hard constraints, contextual risk, bounded scope, freshness, and post-condition verification.
contributions: An executable AC-AZT reference policy that separates agent reasoning from action authority.
A transparent 240-case benchmark with an author-specified three-way authorization oracle.
A paired comparison against direct execution and static role/action authorization using safety, utility, governance, and invariant metrics.
Ablation, threshold, domain, and risk-weight analyses that expose control contributions and calibration trade-offs.
